name: Bough-Stratum
description: Bough-Stratum is a large rocky world whose surface reads like a geological textbook, its strata exposed in layer-cake formations across canyon walls and mountain faces that display the planet's four-billion-year history in bands of color ranging from deep red to pale cream. The thin atmosphere is clear enough to see these formations from orbit, branching canyon networks spreading from central rift valleys like the limbs of a great tree, giving the planet its name. A subterranean ocean locked beneath a kilometers-thick cap of permafrost provides the planet's most valuable resource.

The air on Bough-Stratum is thin enough to require supplemental breathing but thick enough to carry the mineral dust that gives the sunset sky a spectacular range of oranges and pinks. The temperature at the equator can reach comfortable levels during the day, dropping sharply after sunset in the thin atmosphere. Walking the canyon floors, surrounded by walls that display epochs of planetary history in colored bands dozens of meters thick, creates a humbling sense of deep time that visitors describe as almost spiritual.

A terraforming initiative began on Bough-Stratum twenty years ago, installing atmospheric processors in the major canyon systems designed to thicken the atmosphere using gases liberated from the subterranean ocean. The project is functional but decades from completion, and the microbial life that thrives in the subsurface water layer has complicated projections by metabolizing some of the released gases in unexpected ways. The microbes are not interfering with terraforming so much as participating in it, redirecting the atmospheric chemistry along paths the engineers did not anticipate.

Bough-Stratum represents one of the most promising long-term terraforming projects in the sector, with its subterranean water reserves and geothermal potential providing the raw materials for atmospheric generation. The microbial ecosystem's unexpected contributions have attracted biological interest alongside the engineering teams, and a debate has emerged about whether to adapt the terraforming plan to work with the native biology or to sterilize and start fresh. The microbes, indifferent to the debate, continue to reshape the atmosphere on their own terms.
